nodes.name: Hyperbolic pair
nodes.statement: Fix $x \in V$ such that $Q(x) = 0$. Since $Q$ is nondegenerate, there exists $z \in V$ such that $x \cdot z = 1$. The element $y = z - 1/2 \cdot(z\cdot z)x$ is isotropic and $x \cdot y = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Build an isotropic pair with $x\cdot y=1$

nodes.name: Split
nodes.statement: The restriction of $Q$ to the submodule $U := Kx \oplus Ky$ is the desired hyperbolic form $H$. Take $Q'$ to be the restriction of $Q'$ to the orthogonal complement of $U$; then $Q$ is equivalent to $H + Q'$ by Proposition \ref{prop:ortho_compl_properties}(iv).
nodes.statement_short: Split off the hyperbolic plane via Proposition 3(iv)

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $H$ represents all elements of $K$ by Lemma \ref{lem:represents_of_hyperbolic}, so does $Q = H + Q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Hyperbolic part represents everything

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: The forward implication is clear. For the second one, fix a basis for $V$ and assume that $Q' := Q \dotminus rZ$ has a nontrivial zero $(x_1, \cdots, x_n, z) \in V \times K$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a nontrivial zero of $Q\dotminus rZ$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Then either $z = 0$, in which case $Q$ represents zero and thus also $r$, or $Q(x_1/z, \cdots, x_n/z) = r$.
nodes.statement_short: Split on $z=0$ or dehomogenize

nodes.name: (b)<->(c)
nodes.statement: The equivalence (b) $\iff$ (c) follows from Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}. The implication (b) $\implies$ (a) is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: (b)$\iff$(c) from Corollary 1

nodes.name: Case Q(x) nonzero
nodes.statement: To show (a) $\implies (b)$, write a nontrivial zero of $Q \dotminus Q'$ in the form $(x, y)$ with $Q(x) = Q'(y)$. If $Q(x) \ne 0$, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Write the zero as $(x,y)$; case $Q(x)\ne 0$

nodes.name: Case Q(x)=0
nodes.statement: If $Q(x) = 0$, then $Q$ represents $0$ and thus by Proposition \ref{prop:sum_hyperbolic} also all elements of $K$. In particular, it represents all nonzero values taken by $Q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $Q(x)=0$ via Proposition 4

nodes.name: Define epsilon(b)
nodes.statement: Let $b = (b_1, \cdots, b_n)$ be an orthogonal basis for $V$ such that $Q(x) = a_1 x_1^2 + \cdots + a_n x_n^2$ for $x = \sum x_i b_i$. We denote $\epsilon(b) := \prod_{i < j}(a_i, a_j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\epsilon(b)$ for an orthogonal basis

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: If $n=1$, then $\epsilon(f) = 1$. If $n=2$, then $\epsilon(f) = 1$ if and only if the form $Z^2 - a_1 X^2 - a_2 Y^2$ represents $0$. By Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}, this is equivalent to $a_1 X^2 + a_2 Y^2$ representing $1$, which means that there exists $v \in V$ with $Q(v) = 1$; this is independent on $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Ranks 1 and 2 directly

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For $n \ge 3$ we use induction on $n$. By Theorem \ref{thm:exists_chain}, it suffices to prove that for any pair of contiguous bases $b$ and $b'$, we have $\epsilon(b) = \epsilon(b')$. Thanks to the symmetry of the Hilbert symbol, $\epsilon(b)$ is unchanged by permutation of the basis elements, so we may assume that $b_1 = b_1'$. Then $b_1' \cdot b_1' = a_1$, and we can write \begin{align*} \epsilon(b) &= (a_1, a_2 \cdots a_n) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i, a_j) = \\ &= (a_1, d(Q) a_1) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i, a_j). \end{align*} Analogously, \[\epsilon(b') = (a_1', d(Q) a_1) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i', a_j'). \] The result follows by combining $a_1 = a_1'$ and the induction hypothesis applied to the orthogonal complement of $e_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction via contiguous bases

nodes.name: Reduce to contiguous
nodes.statement: For $n \ge 3$ we use induction on $n$. By Theorem \ref{thm:exists_chain}, it suffices to prove that for any pair of contiguous bases $b$ and $b'$, we have $\epsilon(b) = \epsilon(b')$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to contiguous bases via Theorem 11

nodes.name: WLOG
nodes.statement: Thanks to the symmetry of the Hilbert symbol, $\epsilon(b)$ is unchanged by permutation of the basis elements, so we may assume that $b_1 = b_1'$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $b_1=b_1'$

nodes.name: Rewrite
nodes.statement: Then $b_1' \cdot b_1' = a_1$, and we can write \begin{align*} \epsilon(b) &= (a_1, a_2 \cdots a_n) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i, a_j) = \\ &= (a_1, d(Q) a_1) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i, a_j). \end{align*} Analogously, \[\epsilon(b') = (a_1', d(Q) a_1) \prod_{2 \le i < j} (a_i', a_j'). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\epsilon(b)$ and $\epsilon(b')$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result follows by combining $a_1 = a_1'$ and the induction hypothesis applied to the orthogonal complement of $e_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply induction to the orthogonal complement

nodes.name: Diagonalize
nodes.statement: $f$ is equivalent to $aX^2 + bY^2 + cZ^2$ for some $a, b, c \in k^\times$, and $f$ represents $0$ if and only if the form $-caX^2 -cbY^2 - Z^2$ represents $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize and normalize

nodes.name: Symbol identity
nodes.statement: By the definition of Hilbert symbol, this last form represents $0$ if and only if $(-ca, -cb) = 1$. This is equivalent to \[ (-1, -1)(-1, a)(-1, b)(c, c)(a, b)(a, c)(b, c) = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Translate into a Hilbert symbol identity

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:hilbert_symbol_properties} (vi), $(c, c) = (-1, c)$, so this can be rewritten as \[ 1 = (-1, -1)(-1, abc)(a, b)(a, c)(b, c) = (-1, -d(f))\epsilon(f), \] or equivalently, $(-1, -d(f)) = \epsilon(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $(c,c)=(-1,c)$ to reach $(-1,-d(f))=\epsilon(f)$

nodes.name: Reduce to rank 3
nodes.statement: Up to equivalence, we may assume $f = X^2 + bY^2$ for some $b \in k^\times$. By Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}, $f$ represents $a$ if and only if $f_a := f \dotminus aZ^2$ represents $0$, which by Lemma \ref{lem:represents_zero_iff_rk_3} is equivalent to $(-1, -d(f_a)) = \epsilon(f_a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the rank 3 form $f\dotminus aZ^2$

nodes.name: Compute invariants
nodes.statement: A computation shows that $d(f_a) = -a d(f)$ and $\epsilon(f_a) = (a, -d(f)) \epsilon (f)$. Combining this with Proposition \ref{prop:hilbert_symbol_properties}, we conclude the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $d(f_a)$ and $\epsilon(f_a)$

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: $f$ is equivalent to $X_1^2 - aX_2^2$, for some nonzero $a$, which is positive because $f_\infty$ represents $0$. Write \[ a = \prod_p p^{v_p(a)}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Normalize to $X_1^2-aX_2^2$ with $a>0$

nodes.name: Local data
nodes.statement: Since $f_p$ represents $0$, $a$ is a square in $\Q_p$, so $v_p(a)$ is even.
nodes.statement_short: Local isotropy gives even valuations

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It follows that $a$ is a square in $\Q$ and $f$ represents $0$.
nodes.statement_short: $a$ is a rational square

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: $f$ is equivalent to $X_1^2 - a X_2^2 - b X_3^2$; since we can multiply $a$ and $b$ by squares, we can reduce to the case where $a$ and $b$ are square-free integers. We can also assume $|a| \le |b|$. We use induction on $m := |a| + |b|$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize to squarefree $a,b$ and set up induction on $|a|+|b|$

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: If $m = 2$, then $f \sim X_1^2 \pm X_2^2 \pm X_3^2$. The case $X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2$ is excluded by the hypothesis that $f_\infty$ represents zero. In the other cases, $f$ represents zero (take e.g. $(1, 1, 0)$ or $(1, 0, 1)$, respectively).
nodes.statement_short: Base case $m=2$

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $m > 2$, that is, $|b| \ge 2$ and write $b = \pm p_1 \cdots p_k$, where the $p_i$ are distinct primes. Let $p$ be one of the $p_i$; we will show that $a$ is a square modulo $p$. This is obvious if $a \equiv 0 \mod p$. Otherwise $a$ is a $p$-adic unit, and by hypothesis there exists $(x, y, z) \in \Q_p^3$ such that $z^2 - ax^2 - by^2 = 0$. By Proposition \ref{prop:common_root}, we can suppose that $(x, y, z)$ is primitive. From $z^2 - a x^2 \equiv 0 \mod p$, we deduce that if $x \equiv 0 \mod p$, then $z \equiv 0 \mod p$ and $p^2$ divides $by^2$; since $v_p(b) = 1$, this implies $y \equiv 0 \mod p$, contradicting the assumption that $(x, y, z)$ is primitive. Therefore $x \not\equiv 0 \mod p$ and $a$ is a square modulo $p$. Since $\Z / b\Z = \prod_i \Z / p_i \Z$, we also have that $a$ is a square modulo $b$, so there exist integers $t, b'$ such that $bb' = t^2 - a$ and we can choose $t$ so that $|t| \le |b|/2$. Then $bb'$ is a norm of the extension $k(\sqrt{a})/k$ for $k = \Q$, $\R$ or $\Q_p$. From this we conclude that $f$ represents $0$ in $k$ if and only if the same is true for $f' := X_1^2 - a X_2^2 - b' X_3^2$ (see the proof of \cite[\S III.1.1, Proposition 1]{Ser73}). In particular, $f'$ represents $0$ in each $\Q_v$. But we have \[ |b'| = \left | \frac{t^2 - a}{b} \right | \le \frac{|b|}{4} + 1 < |b| \quad \text{because } |b| \ge 2. \] Write $b' = b'' u^2$, with $b'', u$ integers and $b''$ square-free, so $|b''| < |b|$. We can then apply the induction hypothesis to the form $X_1^2 - a X_2^2 - b'' X_3^2$, which is equivalent to $f'$; hence $f'$ represents $0$ in $\Q$ and so does $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Descent from $b$ to smaller $b'$

nodes.name: Fix p
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $m > 2$, that is, $|b| \ge 2$ and write $b = \pm p_1 \cdots p_k$, where the $p_i$ are distinct primes. Let $p$ be one of the $p_i$; we will show that $a$ is a square modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $b$ and fix a prime divisor $p$

nodes.name: Primitive zero
nodes.statement: This is obvious if $a \equiv 0 \mod p$. Otherwise $a$ is a $p$-adic unit, and by hypothesis there exists $(x, y, z) \in \Q_p^3$ such that $z^2 - ax^2 - by^2 = 0$. By Proposition \ref{prop:common_root}, we can suppose that $(x, y, z)$ is primitive.
nodes.statement_short: Take a primitive local zero via Proposition 1

nodes.name: a square mod p
nodes.statement: From $z^2 - a x^2 \equiv 0 \mod p$, we deduce that if $x \equiv 0 \mod p$, then $z \equiv 0 \mod p$ and $p^2$ divides $by^2$; since $v_p(b) = 1$, this implies $y \equiv 0 \mod p$, contradicting the assumption that $(x, y, z)$ is primitive. Therefore $x \not\equiv 0 \mod p$ and $a$ is a square modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $a$ is a square mod $p$

nodes.name: Pass to f'
nodes.statement: Since $\Z / b\Z = \prod_i \Z / p_i \Z$, we also have that $a$ is a square modulo $b$, so there exist integers $t, b'$ such that $bb' = t^2 - a$ and we can choose $t$ so that $|t| \le |b|/2$. Then $bb'$ is a norm of the extension $k(\sqrt{a})/k$ for $k = \Q$, $\R$ or $\Q_p$. From this we conclude that $f$ represents $0$ in $k$ if and only if the same is true for $f' := X_1^2 - a X_2^2 - b' X_3^2$ (see the proof of \cite[\S III.1.1, Proposition 1]{Ser73}).
nodes.statement_short: Write $bb'=t^2-a$, a norm; pass to $f'$

nodes.name: Bound b'
nodes.statement: In particular, $f'$ represents $0$ in each $\Q_v$. But we have \[ |b'| = \left | \frac{t^2 - a}{b} \right | \le \frac{|b|}{4} + 1 < |b| \quad \text{because } |b| \ge 2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|b'|<|b|$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Write $b' = b'' u^2$, with $b'', u$ integers and $b''$ square-free, so $|b''| < |b|$. We can then apply the induction hypothesis to the form $X_1^2 - a X_2^2 - b'' X_3^2$, which is equivalent to $f'$; hence $f'$ represents $0$ in $\Q$ and so does $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply induction to $X_1^2-aX_2^2-b''X_3^2$

nodes.name: Local values
nodes.statement: Up to equivalence, we may assume $f = aX_1^2 + bX_2^2 - (cX_3^2 + dX_4^2)$. Fix a place $v \in V$. Since $f_v$ represents $0$, Corollary \ref{cor:prod_isotropic_iff} shows that there exists $x_v \in \Q_v^\times$ which is represented both by $aX_1^2 + bX_2^2$ and by $cX_3^2 + dX_4^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Local common values $x_v$ via Corollary 2

nodes.name: Symbol conditions
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:represents_iff_rk_2}, this is equivalent to saying that \[ (x_v, -ab)_v = (a, b)_v \quad \text{and} \quad (x_v, -cd)_v = (c, d)_v \: \text{ for all } v \in V. \]
nodes.statement_short: Translate into Hilbert symbol conditions via Lemma 15

nodes.name: Global x
nodes.statement: Since $\displaystyle \prod_{v \in V} (a, b)_v = \prod_{v \in V} (c, d)_v = 1$ by Theorem \ref{thm:product_formula}, we can deduce from Theorem \ref{thm:existence} the existence of $x \in \Q^\times$ such that \[ (x, -ab)_v = (a, b)_v \quad \text{and} \quad (x, -cd)_v = (c, d)_v \: \text{ for all } v \in V. \]
nodes.statement_short: Product formula and existence theorem give a global $x$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This shows that the form $aX_1^2 + bX_2^2 - xZ^2$ represents zero in each $\Q_v$, so by Lemma \ref{lem:isotr_of_rk_three}, it also represents $0$ in $\Q$. By Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}, $x$ is represented by $aX_1^2 + bX_2^2$. The same argument shows that $x$ is represented by $cX_1^2 + dX_2^2$. By applying Corollary \ref{cor:prod_isotropic_iff} again, we conclude that $f$ represents $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rank three case and Corollaries 1-2 conclude

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: The proof uses induction on $n$. Write $f = h - g$, where $h = a_1X_1^2 + a_2X_2^2$, $g = -(a_3X_3^2 + \cdots + a_nX_n^2)$. Let $S$ be the finite subset of $V$ consisting of $\infty, 2$, and the primes $p$ such that $v_p(a_i) \ne 0$ for $i \ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $f=h-g$ and define the finite set $S$

nodes.name: Local values
nodes.statement: Let $v \in S$. Since $f_v$ represents $0$, there exists $c_v \in \Q_v^\times$ which is represented in $\Q_v$ by $h$ and $g$, that is, there exist $x_i^v \in \Q_v$, $i=1, \dots, n$ (with $x_i^v \ne 0$ for $i=1, 2$, and some $i \ge 3$) such that \[ h(x_1^v, x_2^v) = c_v = g(x_3^v, \cdots, x_n^v).\]
nodes.statement_short: Local common values $c_v$

nodes.name: Approximate
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:padic_squares_open}, the squares of $\Q_p^\times$ form an open set. Combining this with the approximation theorem \ref{thm:approximation}, we deduce the existence of $x_1, x_2 \in \Q^\times$ such that, denoting $c := h(x_1, x_2)$, one has $c/c_v \in {\Q_v^\times}^2$ for all $v \in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximation and openness of squares give a rational $c$

nodes.name: Local isotropy of f_1
nodes.statement: Consider the form $f_1 := cZ^2 - g$. For each $v \in S$, $g$ represents $c_v$ in $\Q_v$, and hence also $c$ because $c/c_v \in {\Q_v^\times}^2$, hence $f_1$ represents $0$ in $\Q_v$ by Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}. For $v \notin S$, the coefficients $-a_3, \dots, -a_n$ of $g$ are $v$-adic units, so the discriminant $d_v(g)$ is a $v$-adic unit and $\epsilon_v(g)=1$.

nodes.statement: In all cases, $f_q$ represents $0$ in all $\Q_v$, and since the rank of $f$ is $n-1$, the inductive hypothesis shows that $f_1$ represents $0$ in $\Q$, or equivalently by Corollary \ref{cor:represents_iff_sub_sub}, $g$ represents $c$ in $\Q$. But $h$ also represents $c$, so by Corollary \ref{cor:prod_isotropic_iff} $f$ represents $0$.
